name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38
lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a synthetic lipopeptide used as a cosmetic anti-wrinkle ingredient, applied to the face in serums and creams so that skin looks smoother and firmer. It is sold by Sederma, a subsidiary of Croda, under the trade name Matrixyl Synthe'6, and is described by the supplier as a matrikine mimic, meaning a small signalling fragment intended to prompt the skin to remodel its extracellular matrix.[1]

Its marketing rests on the claim that it stimulates production of collagens I, III and IV, fibronectin, hyaluronic acid and laminin-5, with the stated aim of visibly reducing wrinkle volume and depth, especially on the forehead and around the eyes.[1] The most detailed efficacy figures available come from supplier-described testing (a double-blind study of 25 women using a 2% cream), as reported in an AI-generated encyclopedia summary; independent peer-reviewed trials of the isolated ingredient were not located.[1]

Published human studies that include the peptide test finished serums or moisturizers containing many other active ingredients, so effects cannot be attributed to the peptide alone.[2][3][4] It is a cosmetic ingredient and is not a drug.
infobox: 2% of the supplied blend in emulsions [1]

paras: The ingredient is a palmitoylated tripeptide, with a fatty-acid chain attached to improve compatibility with skin lipids. Supplier information describes it as derived from sequences found in collagen VI and laminins and supplied in a water-soluble blend, with glycerin, water and hydroxypropyl cyclodextrin, for use in emulsions.[1] Grokipedia gives its formula as C33H65N5O7S and a molecular weight of about 676 g/mol and describes it as made by solid-phase peptide synthesis using a non-natural methionine sulfone residue.[1]
It is distinct from other cosmetic peptides such as palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, which have different sequences and claimed functions.[1]

Grokipedia dates development to the early 2010s, with the patent application WO 2010/082175 and claims substantiation documented in September 2010.[1] It sits in the same Sederma line as the older Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, the KTTKS peptide bound to a 16-carbon palmitoyl chain), which Sederma launched in 2000 and which was called palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 before 2006.[7] Wikipedia classes the older peptide as a matrikine, a messenger peptide thought to interact with receptors to regulate cell activity, and notes that its anti-wrinkle mechanism claim carries a request for a medical citation.[7] The Matrixyl line received an in-cosmetics 25 Years of Innovation Award in 2015, according to the supplier.[1]

According to the supplier, the peptide signals the skin to increase synthesis of six components of the dermal-epidermal junction and extracellular matrix, with in vitro assays reporting large percentage increases in collagen I and hyaluronic acid, and an ability to raise skin water content through hyaluronic acid synthesis.[1] These are manufacturer assay results and have not been independently reproduced.

A supplier-reported double-blind study in 25 women aged 42 to 70 applying a 2% cream twice daily for two months reported, versus placebo, a 31 percent average reduction in forehead wrinkle volume, a 16.3 percent decrease in maximum wrinkle depth and a 28 percent lifting effect; for crow's feet the regimen reported a 21.1 percent reduction in wrinkle volume.[1]

Independent studies include the ingredient only as one component of a formula. An open-label trial in 37 women aged 35 to 60 tested a moisturizer containing astragalus root extract, a peptide blend including palmitoyl tripeptide-38, rosemary leaf extract, tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate and coenzyme Q10, applied twice daily with evaluations at 4, 8 and 12 weeks.[2] An open-label study in women aged 40 and over with visible photoaging applied a serum of 15 percent L-ascorbic acid, tocopheryl acetate and 5 ppm palmitoyl tripeptide-38 once daily for 56 days and reported significant decreases of 8 to 9 percent in skin-roughness parameters and increased skin isotropy.[3] An ISDIN serum containing apple stem cell extract, urea, creatine and palmitoyl tripeptide-38 was tested in vitro on senescent fibroblasts and applied twice daily for 28 days in 32 women with sensitive skin.[6]

A face serum containing bakuchiol, palmitoyl tripeptide-38 and hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid was tested in vitro, in a repeat insult patch test in 55 adults and in a human efficacy trial, reported as a preprint.[4] A completed 2025 registered trial examined an AI-personalized skincare regimen for photoaging in 43 women.[5] No trial isolating palmitoyl tripeptide-38 against a vehicle, run independently of the manufacturer, was identified.
The serum study in 55 volunteers reported no irritation or allergic contact dermatitis from its formula.[4] Long-term safety data specific to the peptide are limited.

The ingredient appears in serums, creams and make-up marketed for skin aging, typically listed on labels by its INCI name, palmitoyl tripeptide-38, alongside other peptides.[1] Cosmetic peptides have a place in skincare discussion as an alternative to retinoids for people who want to work on wrinkles without irritation, although the studies above do not compare the two.

card.summary: A branded cosmetic signal peptide sold as a collagen booster; the evidence is mostly supplier data and multi-ingredient serum studies.
card.note: Human studies test whole formulas, not the peptide alone.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a lab-made peptide added to anti-wrinkle serums and creams. The supplier says it prompts skin to make more collagen and hyaluronic acid.
Most efficacy numbers come from the manufacturer. Independent studies test finished products with many ingredients, so the peptide's own contribution is not separated out.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a matrikine mimic: a fragment-like signal meant to trigger the skin's matrix-building cells. A palmitoyl fatty chain is attached to help it mix with skin lipids.
quick.risks: A 55-person patch test of one serum containing it reported no irritation. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug, and long-term data specific to the peptide are limited.

chain: Peptide is applied topically in a serum or cream
Signals matrix-building cells, claimed to raise collagen, fibronectin and hyaluronic acid
Skin looks smoother and firmer, with shallower wrinkles
angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is an ingredient in anti-aging products used to soften the look of wrinkles and improve firmness. The supplier reports wrinkle-volume reductions in its own testing, while independent studies test it only inside multi-ingredient formulas.
